explanations.explanation: Saving him. David asks why God is “…so far from saving me…” and he says it plain. He doesn't dress it up or make it fancy. I think that's the kind of prayer you can only pray when you really need help. And he prays it right when God feels far away.

Not quite, friend. Nobody in this verse is asking about punishment. David asks why God is “…so far from saving me…” and that is a cry for rescue. If you want to find the answer in the verse, look for the word that sounds like a lifeline.

Close to the mark, but not what David says. He doesn't mention a test anywhere in that cry. He asks why God is “…so far from saving me…” and then adds “…so far from my words of groaning?” I think a man who's groaning is looking for help, not a quiz.

Not this time, baker. David says the opposite: “I cry out by day, O my God, but You do not answer…” That is a hard line to pray, and he says it out loud anyway. He goes on to say that by night he has no rest.

That's right. David says, “I cry out by day, O my God, but You do not answer…” So in this moment, he isn't hearing an answer. He says it honestly, and he keeps talking to God anyway. And he can't sleep at night either, which I think is the worst combination.

Delivered. David says, “In You our fathers trusted; they trusted and You delivered them.” Then the next verse says they cried out and were set free. David is reminding himself what God has done before. When you're stuck, a good memory can be the best thing in your pocket.

Not quite. Scattering is not what David remembers. He says Israel's fathers “…trusted and You delivered them.” The next verse says they were “set free” and were “not disappointed.” That's a very different ending from being scattered.

Not this one, friend. David doesn't say God humbled the fathers who trusted Him. He says, “…they trusted and You delivered them.” Then he adds that they cried out and were set free. I think he's holding that up like a photo of better days.

Rescue. The mockers sneer, “He trusts in the LORD, let the LORD deliver him; let the LORD rescue him, since He delights in him.” They're using David's trust as a punchline. It stings, and I think it's meant to. The people laughing in this verse are not the ones to learn from.

Not quite. The mockers don't say the LORD should correct David. They say, “…let the LORD rescue him, since He delights in him.” They throw his trust back in his face. It's the opposite of encouragement.

Not this one, baker. Nobody in the crowd says the LORD should silence David. They sneer, “…let the LORD rescue him, since He delights in him.” It's mockery, not a plan for quiet. I'd say they're loud enough on their own.

Not so, friend. David says, “From birth I was cast upon You; from my mother’s womb You have been my God.” That reaches back long before any crown. He's saying God has been his God from the very start.

Right. David says, “From birth I was cast upon You; from my mother’s womb You have been my God.” That's from the very start of his life. A crown has nothing to do with it. His trust goes back before he could even say a word.

explanations.answer: Trouble is near and no one can help
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. David says, “Be not far from me, for trouble is near and there is no one to help.” He doesn't ask for anything fancy. He needs God close because nobody else is. I think that's a prayer a lot of us have prayed.

explanations.answer: He wants to see a sign from heaven
explanations.explanation: Not quite. David never asks for a sign. He says, “Be not far from me, for trouble is near and there is no one to help.” He wants help, not a show. Besides, the signs aren't what he's missing. Help is.

explanations.answer: His enemies have all run away
explanations.explanation: Not this one, friend. The enemies haven't gone anywhere. A few verses later he says, “Many bulls surround me…” David pleads because trouble is near and no one is there to help. If the enemies had all run off, he'd be having a much better day.

explanations.answer: He is weak and worn out
explanations.explanation: Yes. Water poured out can't be gathered back up, and wax goes soft in the heat. David also says his strength is “dried up like a potsherd” (a piece of broken pottery). Put those pictures together and you see a man with nothing left in the tank. I think he's saying he's about as drained as a person can be.

Not quite, friend. Water that's poured out and wax that melts are not angry pictures. They show something running out. David says his heart “melts away within me.” I think that's what you say when you're empty, not when you're fired up.

Not this time. Nobody gets ready to fight while melting like wax. David says his bones are disjointed and his strength is “dried up like a potsherd.” He sounds like a man who can barely stand, not one lacing up for a battle. I wouldn't bet on wax in a boxing match.

True. David says, “I can count all my bones; they stare and gloat over me.” That's a hard picture, and I think this part of the psalm is heavy. He's showing how worn down he is, with people staring at him while he suffers. It's a lot, and he says it honestly.

Not quite. David does say it: “I can count all my bones…” The verse goes on to say that people “stare and gloat over me.” I think this is one of the heavy parts of the psalm. He doesn't hide how rough it is.

His clothing. David says, “They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing.” They're splitting up his things while he's still standing there. It's a cold moment, and I think it hurts. Casting lots was a way of choosing who got what, and here it's used on a man's clothes.

Not quite, friend. A sword isn't mentioned in this verse. David says, “They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing.” It's his clothes they're taking. Not exactly the kind of loot you'd expect, which makes it feel even colder.

Not this one, baker. There's no crown in this verse at all. David says, “They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing.” It's the clothes off his back. I think that makes the moment feel even more stripped down.

His life. David prays, “Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of wild dogs.” He calls it his “precious life.” That's what's on the line, and he asks God to guard it. When you're in that kind of trouble, you ask for the thing that matters most.

Not quite, friend. David doesn't mention a crown here. He prays, “Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of wild dogs.” What he wants saved is his life. Everything else can wait in line behind that.

Not this one, baker. David isn't worried about his name in this verse. He says, “Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of wild dogs.” It's his life he asks God to save. That's the thing he calls precious.

Proclaim. David says, “I will proclaim Your name to my brothers; I will praise You in the assembly.” That's not a whisper in the corner. He's going to say it out loud where people can hear. Right after the cry, here comes the voice.
Not quite. David doesn't say he'll guard God's name. He says, “I will proclaim Your name to my brothers…” Proclaiming means telling it out loud. He's going to share it, not lock it up.

Not this one, friend. David says, “I will proclaim Your name to my brothers; I will praise You in the assembly.” That's a lot louder than a whisper. I picture him standing up in front of the whole crowd. Whispering is for surprise parties.

Not quite. David doesn't mention priests here. He says, “You who fear the LORD, praise Him!” Then he adds, “All offspring of Israel, revere Him!” He opens the call wide to everyone who fears the LORD.

That's right. David says, “You who fear the LORD, praise Him!” He also says, “All offspring of Israel, revere Him!” No priests are singled out. The invitation is for everybody who fears the LORD. I like a guest list that big.

Yes. David says the LORD “…has not hidden His face from him, but has attended to his cry for help.” That's a reason worth singing about. The one who was crying out was heard. After all those verses of groaning, that's good news.

Not quite, friend. David doesn't say anything about being made a mighty king here. He says the LORD “…has not hidden His face from him, but has attended to his cry for help.” The reason to praise is that God heard. That's plenty.
Not this one, baker. No new name shows up in this verse. David says the LORD has “…attended to his cry for help.” The afflicted one cried out and God paid attention. That's the reason to praise.

The poor. David says, “The poor will eat and be satisfied; those who seek the LORD will praise Him.” They don't just eat, they eat and are satisfied. I think that's a picture of every plate being full and nobody leaving hungry. Think of a cookie box that never runs out.
Not quite, baker. David doesn't say kings in this verse. He says, “The poor will eat and be satisfied…” It's the poor who get the satisfied part. Kings can wait their turn.

Not this one, friend. Priests aren't named in this verse. David says, “The poor will eat and be satisfied…” and then, “those who seek the LORD will praise Him.” The poor are the ones at the table here.

True. David says all the families of the nations will bow down before Him. Then he gives the reason: “For dominion belongs to the LORD and He rules over the nations.” The ruling comes first, and the bowing follows. It's a big, wide picture.

Not quite, friend. David says it right out: “For dominion belongs to the LORD and He rules over the nations.” That comes right after the nations bow down before Him. The word “For” ties them together. He gives the reason on the spot.
Not so, baker. David says, “All the rich of the earth will feast and worship…” They're not left out. They're right there at the feast. The rich are in the picture too.

That's right. David says, “All the rich of the earth will feast and worship…” They're not left out at all. They get a seat at the feast and join the worship. The line goes on to say that those who go down to the dust will kneel before Him too.

His righteousness. David says they will “…proclaim His righteousness…” to a people not yet born. The next generation gets told who God is and what He has done. It's a story passed from one group to the next. I think that's the best kind of handoff.
Not quite, friend. No army shows up in the last verse. David says they will “…proclaim His righteousness…” That's what future generations tell. The story is about who God is and what He has done.

Not this one, baker. David doesn't mention riches in the last verse. He says they will “…proclaim His righteousness…” to people yet unborn. That's the message that gets passed on. It's about what He has done.
